title: A hundred hours from nine
hook: It's 9 o'clock. Do you really have to count 100 hours, one at a time?

doesNotKnow: that remainders make wrap-around (clock) arithmetic: whole laps of 12 can be thrown away

misconception: Finding the time 100 hours later means counting 100 steps one by one; or the remainder itself is the answer.
objective: The learner can split 100 hours into 8 laps of 12 plus 4, explain that the laps leave the hand where it was, and get 9 + 4 = 13, shown as 1 o'clock.

claims.text: On a 12-hour clock, adding 12 hours is one full lap of the hour hand and brings it back to the same number.
claims.source: A 12-hour dial: the hour hand turns 30° per hour, so 12 hours = 360°. Demo.tsx clock(h) = ((9 + h − 1) mod 12) + 1.

claims.text: 100 hours is 8 laps of 12 hours (96 hours) plus 4 hours: 100 = 8 × 12 + 4.
claims.source: Node: Math.floor(100 / 12) = 8, 100 % 12 = 4. Demo.tsx LAPS and LEFT.

claims.text: From 9 o'clock, the last 4 hours move the hand to 10, 11, 12 and then 1, so 100 hours after 9 o'clock it is 1 o'clock (9 + 4 = 13, shown as 1).
On a clock, full laps change nothing; only the remainder after dividing by 12 moves the hand.
claims.source: (t + 12k + r) mod 12 = (t + r) mod 12 for whole k (modular arithmetic; e.g. any number theory text on congruences).

recall.question: It is 5 o'clock on a 12-hour clock. What time is it 50 hours later?
